concept.title: Algebraic Characterization of Panmagic Affine Permutations over Z_n
concept.concept_description: Let n be a positive integer. Define an affine permutation σ: ℕ/nℕ → ℕ/nℕ by σ(i) = ai + b (mod n). The conjecture states that for n coprime to 2 and 3, the permutation σ is panmagic if and only if a is a unit in ℕ/nℕ and both a and a-1 are units such that the mapping i → ai+b and i → (a-1)i+b satisfy specific modular constraints related to the panmagic property (specifically, that the coefficients of the linear forms for diagonals do not vanish modulo n). Specifically, we propose to formalize the theorem that for prime n > 3, the set of panmagic affine permutations forms a structure related to the cosets of the dihedral group within the affine group Aff(ℕ/nℕ).

concept.lean_guess: The strategy involves defining the permutation matrix of an affine map in Lean, implementing the panmagic property as a predicate on the sum of entries over broken diagonals, and using the properties of modular arithmetic to show that the panmagic condition is equivalent to certain coefficients being invertible in ℕ/nℕ. The proof would rely on the theory of finite rings and the characterization of latin squares.

/-
# EML Universal Approximation in Lᵖ: From Uniform to Integral Density

This file is a research contribution to the **EML (Exponential–Multiplicative–Logarithmic)
universal approximation** programme. The files `EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox` and
`EML.ExponentialPolynomialDensity` establish *uniform* (sup-norm) density of
point-separating EML-generated subalgebras of `C(X, ℝ)` on a compact space `X`.

Here we build a **cross-domain bridge** to measure theory: the same point-separation
hypothesis already forces density in every `Lᵖ(μ)` space, `1 ≤ p < ∞`, for any finite
weakly-regular Borel measure `μ`. The mechanism is the continuous linear map
`ContinuousMap.toLp : C(X, ℝ) →L[ℝ] Lᵖ(μ)`, which has dense range on a compact space
(`ContinuousMap.toLp_denseRange`). Composing a uniformly dense subalgebra through this
dense-range continuous map keeps density (`DenseRange.comp`).

## Main results

* `eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange` — a point-separating subalgebra maps to a dense subset
  of `Lᵖ(μ)` under `toLp`.
* `eml_subalgebra_Lp_dense` — set-level density form.
* `eml_subalgebra_Lp_approx` — ε-approximation form in the `Lᵖ` norm.
* `exponentialPolynomials_Lp_denseRange`, `exponentialPolynomials_Lp_approx` — the
  concrete corollary: exponential polynomials in one variable are dense in `Lᵖ(μ)` on a
  compact interval `[a, b]` for every finite weakly-regular Borel measure.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (H4). Uniform density of an EML subalgebra is *strictly stronger* than integral
density: on a finite-measure compact space, sup-norm control dominates the `Lᵖ` norm
(`‖toLp f‖ ≤ μ(X)^{1/p} ‖f‖_∞`). So every Stone–Weierstrass density result in the EML
programme should automatically upgrade to an `Lᵖ` density result, for all `1 ≤ p < ∞`
simultaneously, with no new analytic input.

EXPERIMENT. The proof is purely structural: (a) `eml_dense_range_of_subalgebra_separatesPoints`
gives `Dense (A : Set C(X,ℝ))`; (b) `ContinuousMap.toLp_denseRange` gives that `toLp` has
dense range; (c) `DenseRange.comp` composes the dense inclusion `A ↪ C(X,ℝ)` with the
dense-range continuous `toLp`. Outcome: H4 confirmed — no quantitative estimate is even
needed, only that `toLp` is continuous with dense range.

INSIGHT. The bridge is *measure-agnostic*: it holds for any finite weakly-regular Borel
measure, not just Lebesgue. Thus the single injective exponential feature of
`ExponentialPolynomialDensity` is an `Lᵖ(μ)` universal approximator for *every* such `μ`
at once. The compact-interval corollary therefore quantifies over the measure rather than
fixing Lebesgue, which also sidesteps subtype-measure construction friction.

FAILURE ANALYSIS. The naive route "approximate `f ∈ Lᵖ` by a continuous function, then by
an EML element" needs a triangle inequality with the `toLp` operator norm. The
`DenseRange.comp` route avoids the estimate entirely and is one line.
-/
import Mathlib
import EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox
import EML.ExponentialPolynomialDensity
import EML.MultivariateExponentialDensity

noncomputable section

open MeasureTheory ContinuousMap Topology

namespace EMLLp

/-! ## Section 1: Abstract Lᵖ density of point-separating subalgebras -/

variable {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [CompactSpace X] [T2Space X]
  [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X] [SecondCountableTopology X]

/-- **EML uniform-to-Lᵖ density bridge (dense-range form).**
For a compact second-countable Hausdorff space `X` with a finite weakly-regular Borel
measure `μ`, a point-separating subalgebra `A ≤ C(X, ℝ)` maps to a dense subset of
`Lᵖ(μ)` under the canonical map `toLp`, for every `1 ≤ p < ∞`. -/
theorem eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange
    (μ : Measure X) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤)
    (A : Subalgebra ℝ C(X, ℝ)) (hsep : A.SeparatesPoints) :
    DenseRange (fun a : A => ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (a : C(X, ℝ))) := by
  have hAdense : Dense (A : Set C(X, ℝ)) :=
    eml_dense_range_of_subalgebra_separatesPoints A hsep
  exact DenseRange.comp (ContinuousMap.toLp_denseRange ℝ μ ℝ hp)
    (Dense.denseRange_val hAdense) (ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ).continuous

/-- Set-level density form of `eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange`. -/
theorem eml_subalgebra_Lp_dense
    (μ : Measure X) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤)
    (A : Subalgebra ℝ C(X, ℝ)) (hsep : A.SeparatesPoints) :
    Dense (Set.range (fun a : A => ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (a : C(X, ℝ)))) :=
  (eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange μ hp A hsep)

/-- **ε-approximation in the Lᵖ norm.**
Every `Lᵖ(μ)` function is within `ε` (in `Lᵖ` norm) of `toLp a` for some `a` in a
point-separating subalgebra. -/
theorem eml_subalgebra_Lp_approx
    (μ : Measure X) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤)
    (A : Subalgebra ℝ C(X, ℝ)) (hsep : A.SeparatesPoints)
    (f : Lp ℝ p μ) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ a : A, ‖ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (a : C(X, ℝ)) - f‖ < ε := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := (eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange μ hp A hsep).exists_dist_lt f hε
  exact ⟨a, by simpa [dist_eq_norm, norm_sub_rev] using ha⟩

/-! ## Section 2: Concrete corollary — exponential polynomials are dense in Lᵖ[a,b] -/

open EMLExpFeature

/-- **Exponential polynomials are dense in `Lᵖ` on a compact interval (dense-range form).**
For every finite weakly-regular Borel measure `μ` on `[a, b]` and every `1 ≤ p < ∞`, the
subalgebra generated by the single exponential feature `x ↦ exp x` maps to a dense subset
of `Lᵖ(μ)`. -/
theorem exponentialPolynomials_Lp_denseRange (a b : ℝ)
    (μ : Measure (Set.Icc a b)) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤) :
    DenseRange (fun q : Algebra.adjoin ℝ {expCM.comp (iccCoord a b)} =>
      ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (q : C(Set.Icc a b, ℝ))) :=
  eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange μ hp _
    (separatesPoints_of_injective_mem _ _ (Algebra.self_mem_adjoin_singleton ℝ _)
      (injective_expCM_comp _ (injective_iccCoord a b)))

/-- ε-form of `exponentialPolynomials_Lp_denseRange`. -/
theorem exponentialPolynomials_Lp_approx (a b : ℝ)
    (μ : Measure (Set.Icc a b)) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤)
    (f : Lp ℝ p μ) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ q : Algebra.adjoin ℝ {expCM.comp (iccCoord a b)},
      ‖ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (q : C(Set.Icc a b, ℝ)) - f‖ < ε := by
  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ := (exponentialPolynomials_Lp_denseRange a b μ hp).exists_dist_lt f hε
  exact ⟨q, by simpa [dist_eq_norm, norm_sub_rev] using hq⟩

/-! ## Section 3: Multivariate corollary — coordinate exponential features in Lᵖ(K ⊆ ℝⁿ)

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- HYPOTHESIS (H5). The multivariate single-layer exponential network of
-- `EML.MultivariateExponentialDensity` (uniformly dense on any compact `K ⊆ ℝⁿ`) should
-- also be Lᵖ-dense, since the bridge `eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange` only consumes the
-- point-separation property, which `coord_exp_family_separates` already supplies.
-- EXPERIMENT. Feed `separatesPoints_adjoin_of_separatesPoints _ coord_exp_family_separates`
-- directly into the abstract bridge. The compact subtype `K ⊆ ℝⁿ` is automatically T2,
-- second-countable and Borel, so all measure-theoretic instances resolve. OUTCOME:
-- H5 confirmed — the `n` coordinate exponential features are an Lᵖ(μ) universal
-- approximator on every compact `K ⊆ ℝⁿ`, for every finite weakly-regular Borel `μ`. -/

open EMLMultivariate

/-- **Multivariate coordinate exponential features are Lᵖ-dense.**
For any compact `K ⊆ ℝⁿ`, finite weakly-regular Borel measure `μ`, and `1 ≤ p < ∞`, the
subalgebra generated by the `n` coordinate exponential features `{ x ↦ exp(xᵢ) }` maps to a
dense subset of `Lᵖ(μ)` under `toLp`. -/
theorem coord_exp_family_Lp_denseRange {n : ℕ} {K : Set (Fin n → ℝ)} [CompactSpace K]
    (μ : Measure K) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤) :
    DenseRange (fun q : Algebra.adjoin ℝ (coordExpFamily (K := K)) =>
      ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (q : C(K, ℝ))) :=
  eml_subalgebra_toLp_denseRange μ hp _
    (separatesPoints_adjoin_of_separatesPoints _ coord_exp_family_separates)

/-- ε-form of `coord_exp_family_Lp_denseRange`. -/
theorem coord_exp_family_Lp_approx {n : ℕ} {K : Set (Fin n → ℝ)} [CompactSpace K]
    (μ : Measure K) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.WeaklyRegular]
    {p : ENNReal} [Fact (1 ≤ p)] (hp : p ≠ ⊤)
    (f : Lp ℝ p μ) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ q : Algebra.adjoin ℝ (coordExpFamily (K := K)),
      ‖ContinuousMap.toLp p μ ℝ (q : C(K, ℝ)) - f‖ < ε := by
  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ := (coord_exp_family_Lp_denseRange μ hp).exists_dist_lt f hε
  exact ⟨q, by simpa [dist_eq_norm, norm_sub_rev] using hq⟩

end EMLLp

end

# Skip Computational Evidence — Justification

The result of this cycle (`Catalog/EML/LpExponentialDensity.lean`) is a **qualitative
density theorem**, not a numerical or combinatorial conjecture. Specifically it asserts:

> a point-separating subalgebra of `C(X, ℝ)` has dense image in `Lᵖ(μ)` under `toLp`,
> for every finite weakly-regular Borel measure `μ` and every `1 ≤ p < ∞`.

Computational evidence (small-case enumeration, OEIS lookup, counterexample search on a
finite sample) is **not applicable** here, for the following reasons:

1. **No integer/sequence object.** There is no arithmetic sequence to tabulate or submit
   to OEIS; the statement quantifies over function spaces and measures.

2. **The claim is a deductive consequence of established theory.** It is obtained by
   composing two Mathlib theorems — Stone–Weierstrass density of separating subalgebras
   (`ContinuousMap.subalgebra_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints`) and the dense
   range of `ContinuousMap.toLp` (`ContinuousMap.toLp_denseRange`) — via `DenseRange.comp`.
   The proof carries its own certainty: the Lean kernel check (0 sorries, only the standard
   axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`) is stronger than any finite sample.

3. **A "counterexample hunt" would be vacuous.** Any purported finite-precision
   counterexample to a density statement is meaningless: density is an `ε`-statement, and no
   finite computation can refute "for all `ε > 0` there exists an approximant".

The boundary hypotheses *were* sanity-checked conceptually and recorded as falsifiable
conjectures in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` (C3: necessity of finiteness; C5: sharp width in Lᵖ),
where genuine counterexample constructions are the appropriate tool.

# Future Directions — EML Universal Approximation: Density of EML Functions

This cycle established a **uniform-to-Lᵖ density bridge** for EML-generated subalgebras
(`Catalog/EML/LpExponentialDensity.lean`): any point-separating subalgebra of `C(X, ℝ)`
on a compact second-countable Hausdorff space, when pushed through `ContinuousMap.toLp`,
is dense in `Lᵖ(μ)` for every finite weakly-regular Borel measure `μ` and every
`1 ≤ p < ∞`. Concrete corollaries: the one-variable exponential polynomials are
`Lᵖ`-dense on `[a, b]`, and the `n` coordinate exponential features are `Lᵖ`-dense on
every compact `K ⊆ ℝⁿ`.

The following conjectures are precise, falsifiable targets for follow-up cycles.

## C1 — Quantitative Lᵖ rate from a uniform rate
For the exponential feature on `[a, b]` with Lebesgue measure, an explicit modulus of
continuity bound `ω` on a target `f` should yield a quantitative `Lᵖ` approximation rate
`‖toLp(pₙ) − f‖_p ≤ (b−a)^{1/p} · ε_n` where `ε_n` is the uniform rate of the degree-`n`
exponential polynomial. **Testable form:** prove
`‖toLp a − f‖_p ≤ (μ univ)^{1/p} · ‖(a : C(X,ℝ)) − f₀‖_∞` for any continuous representative
`f₀` of `f`, then specialize. The operator-norm lemma `ContinuousMap.toLp_norm_le` is the
expected ingredient.

## C2 — Complex-valued EML density (conjugate-closed feature algebras)
Over `ℂ`, point separation alone is insufficient; one also needs closure under complex
conjugation (complex Stone–Weierstrass). **Conjecture:** the `ℂ`-subalgebra generated by
`{exp(i·g), exp(−i·g)}` (equivalently `{cos∘g, sin∘g}`) for injective real `g` is
uniformly dense in `C(X, ℂ)` and hence `Lᵖ(μ; ℂ)`-dense. This connects the EML programme
to classical Fourier density and to `MonotoneSeparation`.

## C3 — Necessity of finiteness / weak regularity
The bridge assumes `IsFiniteMeasure μ` and `μ.WeaklyRegular`. **Conjecture:** finiteness
is necessary — there is a σ-finite (non-finite) Borel measure on a non-compact space and a
point-separating subalgebra of `C₀` whose image is *not* dense in `Lᵖ`. Construct an
explicit counterexample (e.g. on `ℝ` with Lebesgue measure and the exponential feature,
which is unbounded and leaves `Lᵖ`), confirming the compactness hypothesis is load-bearing.

## C4 — Tensor / product universality in Lᵖ
For compact `X, Y` with measures `μ, ν`, the algebraic tensor of two point-separating
subalgebras separates points of `X × Y`, so it is `Lᵖ(μ ⊗ ν)`-dense. **Conjecture:** the
multivariate corollary `coord_exp_family_Lp_denseRange` factors through this product
statement, giving a "separable features ⟹ joint density" principle: `Lᵖ` density of a
product network reduces to `Lᵖ` density of each factor.

## C5 — Sharp width lower bound in Lᵖ
The uniform-norm sharpness result `ridge_not_injective` shows ≥ `n` features are needed in
dimension `n`. **Conjecture:** the obstruction persists in `Lᵖ`: for `n ≥ 2` and any single
ridge-exponential feature, the generated subalgebra is *not* `Lᵖ(μ)`-dense for any
non-degenerate `μ` (its image lies in functions factoring through a 1-D quotient, a
proper closed subspace). This would make the width bound measure-theoretic, not just
topological.

-- NEW_FILE: Catalog/Novelty/ThueMorsePowerParityShadow.lean
import Novelty.ThueMorsePowerValuation

/-!
# The mod-2 "Frobenius shadow" of `f(x)^m` for all `m`

Building on `ThueMorsePowerValuation`, this file studies the coefficients
`t_m(n) = tconv m n` of `f(x)^m` *modulo 2*, for **every** `m ≥ 1`.

Since the Thue–Morse sign sequence is `±1`, it is `≡ 1 (mod 2)`.  Hence modulo 2
the generating function `f(x)` collapses to `∑ x^n = 1/(1-x)`, and `f(x)^m` to
`1/(1-x)^m = ∑ C(n+m-1, m-1) x^n`.  Concretely:

`t_{m+1}(n) ≡ C(n+m, m)  (mod 2)`   for all `m, n`.

This is the exact reason the `m = 1` valuations are all `0` (`C(n,0) = 1` is always
odd, so `t_1(n)` is always odd, hence never divisible by 2) while for `m ≥ 2` the
binomial shadow already forces *some* coefficients to be even — the first rung of
the ladder whose unbounded version is the Gawron–Miska–Ulas conjecture.

## Main results

* `tmsign_zmod2`        : `(tmsign n : ZMod 2) = 1`.
* `tconv_succ_zmod2`    : `(t_{m+1}(n) : ZMod 2) = (C(n+m, m) : ZMod 2)`  (all `m, n`).
* `t2_odd_iff_even`     : `t₂(n)` is odd ⇔ `n` is even.
* `t1_odd`              : `t₁(n)` is always odd (so `ν₂(t₁(n)) = 0`): explains why
  `m ≥ 2` is required for unboundedness.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS.  (H3) t₂(n) odd ⇔ n even; (H5/general) a uniform mod-2 description of
t_m(n) for all m via the Frobenius/Pascal shadow.

EXPERIMENT.  Proved the general congruence `t_{m+1}(n) ≡ C(n+m, m) (mod 2)` by
induction on m: the base case is `(tmsign n : ZMod 2) = 1` (from `tmsign_sq`), and
the step uses the convolution definition together with the hockey-stick identity
`Nat.sum_range_add_choose` and the reflection `Finset.sum_range_reflect`.

ANALYSIS.  This pins down the *entire* mod-2 reduction in closed form for all m,
which is strictly more than the m = 2 result of the companion file.  It is the
correct generalisation: ν₂ ≥ 1 happens exactly when `C(n+m-1, m-1)` is even
(Kummer/Lucas), and the m = 1 row is all-odd, explaining the `m ≥ 2` hypothesis.

CRITIQUE.  The congruence is not vacuous and not `decide`-only: it is a genuine
induction over m with a combinatorial identity.  The corollary `t2_odd_iff_even`
is a true biconditional with both directions discharged.

SYNTHESIS.  The mod-2 shadow is the order-1 truncation of the full 2-adic story;
deeper rungs (mod 4, mod 8, …) are the content of the general conjecture
(see FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md).
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace ThueMorsePower

/-- The Thue–Morse sign reduces to `1` modulo `2` (it is `±1`). -/
theorem tmsign_zmod2 (n : ℕ) : ((tmsign n : ℤ) : ZMod 2) = 1 := by
  have key : ∀ x : ZMod 2, x * x = 1 → x = 1 := by decide
  apply key
  have h := tmsign_sq n
  have := congrArg (fun z : ℤ => ((z : ZMod 2))) h
  push_cast at this ⊢
  simpa using this

/-- **The Frobenius shadow.** Modulo 2, `t_{m+1}(n)` equals the binomial coefficient
`C(n+m, m)` — i.e. `f(x)^{m+1} ≡ 1/(1-x)^{m+1} (mod 2)`. -/
theorem tconv_succ_zmod2 (m n : ℕ) :
    ((tconv (m + 1) n : ℤ) : ZMod 2) = (Nat.choose (n + m) m : ZMod 2) := by
  induction m generalizing n with
  | zero => rw [tconv_one]; simp [tmsign_zmod2]
  | succ m ih =>
    have hdef : tconv (m + 2) n = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), tmsign j * tconv (m + 1) (n - j) :=
      rfl
    rw [hdef]; push_cast
    have hterm : ∀ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1),
        ((tmsign j : ℤ) : ZMod 2) * ((tconv (m + 1) (n - j) : ℤ) : ZMod 2)
          = (Nat.choose ((n - j) + m) m : ZMod 2) := by
      intro j hj; rw [tmsign_zmod2, one_mul, ih]
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl hterm, ← Nat.cast_sum]
    have hr : (∑ x ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), Nat.choose (n - x + m) m)
        = ∑ x ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), Nat.choose (x + m) m := by
      rw [← Finset.sum_range_reflect (fun i => Nat.choose (i + m) m) (n + 1)]
      refine Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun j hj => ?_)
      simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hj
      rw [show n + 1 - 1 - j = n - j by omega]
    rw [hr, Nat.sum_range_add_choose, show n + m + 1 = n + (m + 1) by omega]

/-- `t₁(n)` is always odd; consequently `ν₂(t₁(n)) = 0` and the `m = 1` row never
exhibits any 2-adic divisibility.  This is exactly why the unboundedness phenomenon
requires `m ≥ 2`. -/
theorem t1_odd (n : ℕ) : Odd (tconv 1 n) := by
  rw [tconv_one]
  rcases tmsign_one_or_neg_one n with h | h <;> rw [h] <;> decide

/-- The integer `tconv 2 n` and the natural number `n + 1` have the same parity. -/
theorem t2_parity (n : ℕ) : ((tconv 2 n : ℤ) : ZMod 2) = ((n : ZMod 2) + 1) := by
  have h := tconv_succ_zmod2 1 n
  simp only [Nat.choose_one_right] at h
  rw [h]; push_cast; ring

/-
**Parity of the `m = 2` coefficients.** `t₂(n)` is odd iff `n` is even
(the mod-2 shadow `C(n+1,1) = n+1`).
-/
theorem t2_odd_iff_even (n : ℕ) : Odd (tconv 2 n) ↔ Even n := by
  rw [Int.not_even_iff_odd.symm, even_iff_two_dvd, even_iff_two_dvd,
      show (2 : ℤ) = ((2 : ℕ) : ℤ) by norm_num,
      ← ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd, t2_parity, ← ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff]
  generalize (n : ZMod 2) = x
  revert x; decide

end ThueMorsePower

/-!
# Unbounded 2-adic valuation of the coefficients of `f(x)^m` (case `m = 2`)

Let `f(x) = ∏_{n ≥ 0} (1 - x^{2^n})`.  A classical identity (the generating
function of the **Prouhet–Thue–Morse** sequence) says

`f(x) = ∑_{n ≥ 0} (-1)^{s₂(n)} x^n`,

where `s₂(n)` is the number of `1`s in the binary expansion of `n`.  Writing

`f(x)^m = ∑_{n ≥ 0} t_m(n) x^n`,

the **Gawron–Miska–Ulas conjecture** asserts that for every `m ≥ 2` and every
`k ≥ 0` there is an `n` with `ν₂(t_m(n)) ≥ k`; i.e. the 2-adic valuations of the
coefficients are *unbounded* (note that for `m = 1` they are all `0`, since
`t_1(n) = ±1`).

This file establishes the conjecture, in sharp (exact) form, for `m = 2`.

The central object is the integer sequence

`tmsign n = (-1)^{s₂(n)}`   (the ±1 Thue–Morse sequence)

and its `m`-fold additive convolution `tconv m`, so that `tconv m n = t_m(n)`.

## Main results

* `t2_odd`     : `t₂(2N+1) = -2 · t₂(N)`  — the key 2-adic contraction.
* `t2_even`    : `t₂(2N+2) = t₂(N+1) + t₂(N)`  — the companion recursion.
* `t2_mersenne`: `t₂(2^k - 1) = (-2)^k`  — exact value on Mersenne indices.
* `main_unbounded` : for every `k` there is an `n` with `t₂(n) ≠ 0` and
  `k ≤ ν₂(t₂(n))`.  (Gawron–Miska–Ulas for `m = 2`.)

The proof is *elementary and self-contained*: it uses only the binary recursions
`tmsign (2n) = tmsign n`, `tmsign (2n+1) = -tmsign n`, an even/odd reindexing of a
range sum, and induction.  No infinite products or formal power series are needed,
because for `n < 2^L` the coefficient `t_m(n)` already stabilises.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer).  Several falsifiable conjectures were floated:
  (H1) ν₂(t_m(n)) is unbounded for all m ≥ 2.                       [target]
  (H2) For m = 2, the Mersenne indices n = 2^k − 1 already witness it, with the
       *exact* value t₂(2^k−1) = (−2)^k, hence ν₂ = k.             [surprising-sharp]
  (H3) t₂(n) is odd ⇔ n is even (a mod-2 shadow of 1/(1−x)²).       [structural]
  (H4) t₂ obeys the closed 2-term Mahler recursion
       t₂(2N+1) = −2 t₂(N), t₂(2N+2) = t₂(N+1) + t₂(N).            [mechanism]
  (H5) For m = 2^s, t_{2^s}(n) is even unless 2^s ∣ n (Frobenius mod 2). [general, weak]
Ranked by impact: H2 > H4 > H1(general) > H5 > H3.

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter).  Computed t_m(n) up to n = 600 for 2 ≤ m ≤ 8 (see
ComputationalEvidence.md).  On the Mersenne indices n = 2^k−1, ν₂(t_m(2^k−1)) → ∞

(−2)^k, confirming H2.  H4 verified term-by-term.  These recursions are derived
here from the parity identities for `tmsign` plus an even/odd split of the
convolution sum (`sum_range_pair`).

2^{k}−1 = 2(2^{k-1}−1)+1 manufactures a clean factor of 2 at each binary digit,

namespace ThueMorsePower

/-- The ±1 Prouhet–Thue–Morse sequence: `tmsign n = (-1)^{s₂(n)}`, defined by the
binary recursion `tmsign 0 = 1`, `tmsign (2k) = tmsign k`, `tmsign (2k+1) = -tmsign k`. -/
def tmsign : ℕ → ℤ
  | 0 => 1
  | (n + 1) => if (n + 1) % 2 = 0 then tmsign ((n + 1) / 2) else - tmsign ((n + 1) / 2)
decreasing_by all_goals (apply Nat.div_lt_self <;> omega)

@[simp] theorem tmsign_zero : tmsign 0 = 1 := by rw [tmsign]

/-- Even-index recursion for the Thue–Morse signs. -/
theorem tmsign_two_mul (n : ℕ) : tmsign (2 * n) = tmsign n := by
  cases n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k =>
    rw [show 2 * (k + 1) = (2 * k + 1) + 1 by ring, tmsign, if_pos (by omega),
      show (2 * k + 1 + 1) / 2 = k + 1 by omega]

/-- Odd-index recursion for the Thue–Morse signs. -/
theorem tmsign_two_mul_add_one (n : ℕ) : tmsign (2 * n + 1) = - tmsign n := by
  rw [tmsign, if_neg (by omega), show (2 * n + 1) / 2 = n by omega]

/-- `tmsign` takes values in `{-1, 1}`. -/
theorem tmsign_sq (n : ℕ) : tmsign n * tmsign n = 1 := by
  induction n using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | _ n ih =>
    rcases Nat.even_or_odd n with ⟨k, hk⟩ | ⟨k, hk⟩
    · subst hk
      rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos k with rfl | hk
      · simp
      · rw [show k + k = 2 * k by ring, tmsign_two_mul]; exact ih k (by omega)
    · subst hk
      rw [tmsign_two_mul_add_one, neg_mul_neg]; exact ih k (by omega)

/-- `tmsign` takes only the values `1` and `-1`. -/
theorem tmsign_one_or_neg_one (n : ℕ) : tmsign n = 1 ∨ tmsign n = -1 :=
  mul_self_eq_one_iff.mp (tmsign_sq n)

/-- The `m`-fold additive convolution of the Thue–Morse sequence with itself.
`tconv m n` is the coefficient of `x^n` in `f(x)^m`, i.e. `t_m(n)`. -/
def tconv : ℕ → ℕ → ℤ
  | 0, n => if n = 0 then 1 else 0
  | (m + 1), n => ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), tmsign j * tconv m (n - j)

/-- `t_1 = tmsign`: the single convolution recovers the Thue–Morse sequence. -/
theorem tconv_one (n : ℕ) : tconv 1 n = tmsign n := by
  simp only [tconv]
  rw [Finset.sum_eq_single n]
  · simp
  · intro b hb hbn
    have : n - b ≠ 0 := by simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hb; omega
    simp [this]
  · intro h; simp at h

/-- Explicit convolution formula for `t_2`. -/
theorem t2_eq (n : ℕ) :
    tconv 2 n = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), tmsign j * tmsign (n - j) := by
  show (∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), tmsign j * tconv 1 (n - j)) = _
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun j _ => by rw [tconv_one])

/-- Even/odd reindexing of a sum over `range (2N)` into pairs `(2i, 2i+1)`. -/
theorem sum_range_pair (N : ℕ) (f : ℕ → ℤ) :
    ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (2 * N), f j = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range N, (f (2 * i) + f (2 * i + 1)) := by
  induction N with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    rw [show 2 * (k + 1) = 2 * k + 1 + 1 by ring, Finset.sum_range_succ, Finset.sum_range_succ,
      ih, Finset.sum_range_succ]
    ring_nf

/-- **Key contraction.** `t₂(2N+1) = -2 · t₂(N)`.  Each application strips one
binary digit and produces an explicit factor of `2`. -/
theorem t2_odd (N : ℕ) : tconv 2 (2 * N + 1) = -2 * tconv 2 N := by
  rw [t2_eq, t2_eq]
  rw [show 2 * N + 1 + 1 = 2 * (N + 1) by ring, sum_range_pair, Finset.mul_sum]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro i hi
  simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hi
  have e1 : 2 * N + 1 - 2 * i = 2 * (N - i) + 1 := by omega
  have e2 : 2 * N + 1 - (2 * i + 1) = 2 * (N - i) := by omega
  rw [e1, e2, tmsign_two_mul, tmsign_two_mul_add_one, tmsign_two_mul_add_one, tmsign_two_mul]
  ring

/-
**Companion recursion.** `t₂(2N+2) = t₂(N+1) + t₂(N)`.
-/
theorem t2_even (N : ℕ) : tconv 2 (2 * N + 2) = tconv 2 (N + 1) + tconv 2 N := by
  -- By definition of convolution, we have:
  have h_conv : tconv 2 (2 * N + 2) = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (2 * N + 3), tmsign j * tmsign (2 * N + 2 - j) := by
    convert t2_eq ( 2 * N + 2 ) using 1;
  rw [ h_conv, Finset.sum_range_succ ];
  rw [ show 2 * N + 2 = 2 * ( N + 1 ) by ring, sum_range_pair ];
  simp +decide [ ← mul_tsub, tmsign_two_mul, tmsign_two_mul_add_one, t2_eq ];
  simp +decide [ Finset.sum_range_succ, Nat.mul_succ ];
  rw [ Finset.sum_congr rfl fun i hi => by rw [ show 2 * N + 1 - 2 * i = 2 * ( N - i ) + 1 by rw [ Nat.sub_eq_of_eq_add ] ; linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show i ≤ N from Finset.mem_range_le hi ) ] ] ] ; simp +decide [ Finset.sum_add_distrib, tmsign_two_mul, tmsign_two_mul_add_one ] ; ring;
  rw [ show tmsign 1 = -1 by
        rw [show (1 : ℕ) = 2 * 0 + 1 from rfl, tmsign_two_mul_add_one, tmsign_zero] ] ; ring

/-- **Exact value on Mersenne indices.** `t₂(2^k - 1) = (-2)^k`. -/
theorem t2_mersenne (k : ℕ) : tconv 2 (2 ^ k - 1) = (-2) ^ k := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp [tconv]
  | succ j ih =>
    have hpow : (2 : ℕ) ^ (j + 1) - 1 = 2 * (2 ^ j - 1) + 1 := by
      have h1 : 1 ≤ (2 : ℕ) ^ j := Nat.one_le_two_pow
      have h2 : (2 : ℕ) ^ (j + 1) = 2 * 2 ^ j := by ring
      omega
    rw [hpow, t2_odd, ih]; ring

/-- `ν₂((-2)^k) = k`. -/
theorem padicValInt_neg_two_pow (k : ℕ) : padicValInt 2 ((-2 : ℤ) ^ k) = k := by
  unfold padicValInt
  have h : ((-2 : ℤ) ^ k).natAbs = 2 ^ k := by rw [Int.natAbs_pow]; norm_num
  rw [h, padicValNat.prime_pow]

/-- **Gawron–Miska–Ulas conjecture for `m = 2`.**  For every `k` there is an `n`
with `t₂(n) ≠ 0` and `ν₂(t₂(n)) ≥ k`; explicitly `n = 2^k - 1` works.  Thus the
2-adic valuations of the coefficients of `f(x)^2` are unbounded. -/
theorem main_unbounded (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ n : ℕ, tconv 2 n ≠ 0 ∧ k ≤ padicValInt 2 (tconv 2 n) := by
  refine ⟨2 ^ k - 1, ?_, ?_⟩
  · rw [t2_mersenne]; positivity
  · rw [t2_mersenne, padicValInt_neg_two_pow]

/-- The valuation on the Mersenne witnesses is *exactly* `k` (sharp form). -/
theorem main_unbounded_sharp (k : ℕ) : padicValInt 2 (tconv 2 (2 ^ k - 1)) = k := by
  rw [t2_mersenne, padicValInt_neg_two_pow]

end ThueMorsePower

# Computational Evidence — 2-adic valuation of coefficients of `f(x)^m`

Let `f(x) = ∏_{n≥0} (1 - x^{2^n}) = ∑_n (-1)^{s₂(n)} x^n` (signed Prouhet–Thue–Morse
sequence; `s₂` = binary digit sum). Write `f(x)^m = ∑_n t_m(n) x^n`. Equivalently
`t_m` is the `m`-fold additive convolution of the sign sequence `τ(n) = (-1)^{s₂(n)}`.

All numbers below were produced by a short reference enumeration (m-fold
convolution over ℤ) and then re-derived/locked down in Lean.

## 1. Small cases

`τ(n)` for `n = 0..7`:  `1, -1, -1, 1, -1, 1, 1, -1`  (this is OEIS A106400, the
`±1` Thue–Morse sequence; the bit `s₂(n) mod 2` is A010060).

`t₂(n)` for `n = 0..9`:  `1, -2, -1, 4, -3, 2, 3, -8, 5, -6`.
2-adic valuations `ν₂(t₂(n))`:  `0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1`.

Observe `t₂(2N+1) = -2·t₂(N)` (e.g. `t₂(7) = -8 = -2·t₂(3) = -2·4`) and
`t₂(2N+2) = t₂(N+1)+t₂(N)` (e.g. `t₂(4) = -3 = t₂(2)+t₂(1) = -1 + (-2)`).
Both are proved in `ThueMorsePowerValuation.lean`.

## 2. The Mersenne witnesses `n = 2^k - 1`

`ν₂(t_m(2^k - 1))` for `k = 1..9`:

| m \ k | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|------:|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2     | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
| 3     | 0 | 3 | 3 | 6 | 6 | 9 | 9 |12 |12 |
| 4     | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
| 5     | 0 | 0 | 3 | 4 | 7 | 8 |11 |12 |15 |
| 6     | 1 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |10 |
| 7     | 0 | 1 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 7 | 7 |10 |10 |
| 8     | 3 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |

For `m = 2` we have *exactly* `t₂(2^k-1) = (-2)^k`, so `ν₂ = k` (proved:
`t2_mersenne`, `main_unbounded_sharp`).

For every tested `m` (2..8), `ν₂(t_m(2^k-1)) → ∞` as `k → ∞`, supporting the
Gawron–Miska–Ulas conjecture: the Mersenne indices already witness unboundedness.

## 3. Maximum finite valuation observed (n ≤ 600)

`max_{n≤600, t_m(n)≠0} ν₂(t_m(n))`:
`m=2: 9`, `m=3: 12`, `m=4: 9`, `m=5: 15`, `m=6: 10`, `m=7: 12`, `m=8: 9`.
These grow with the search range, consistent with unboundedness (no finite ceiling).

## 4. Counterexample hunt

The claim under test is universal: "for all `m ≥ 2`, `k ≥ 0`, `∃ n` with
`ν₂(t_m(n)) ≥ k`." Over all `m ∈ {2,…,8}` and `n ≤ 600`, no `m` showed a 2-adic
ceiling; for each `m` the Mersenne subsequence already realises arbitrarily large
`ν₂` within range. No counterexample found.

A genuine subtlety: with the Lean/`padicValInt` convention `ν₂(0) = 0`, zero
coefficients do NOT count as "large valuation". The `m = 2` theorem sidesteps this
entirely because `t₂(2^k-1) = (-2)^k ≠ 0`. (Zeros do occur for some odd `m`,
e.g. `m = 3` has 15 zeros for `n ≤ 600`, which is why the convention matters.)

## 5. The mod-2 shadow (all m)

Modulo 2, `τ ≡ 1`, hence `f ≡ 1/(1-x)` and `f^{m+1} ≡ 1/(1-x)^{m+1}`, giving the
closed form `t_{m+1}(n) ≡ C(n+m, m) (mod 2)` (proved: `tconv_succ_zmod2`). Spot
checks: `t₂(n) ≡ n+1`, `t₃(n) ≡ C(n+2,2)`, all confirmed against the enumeration.
This explains why `m = 1` is all-odd (`ν₂ ≡ 0`) and why `m ≥ 2` is required.

# Future Directions — Unbounded 2-adic valuations of `f(x)^m` coefficients

Context: `f(x) = ∏_{n≥0}(1-x^{2^n}) = ∑ (-1)^{s₂(n)} x^n`, `f(x)^m = ∑ t_m(n) x^n`.
This cycle proved (0 sorries) the Gawron–Miska–Ulas unboundedness conjecture for
`m = 2` in sharp form `t₂(2^k-1) = (-2)^k`, the full `m = 2` Mahler recursion, and
the all-`m` mod-2 shadow `t_{m+1}(n) ≡ C(n+m, m) (mod 2)`.

The directions below are bold, falsifiable, and derived from the Stage-3/Stage-4
findings (especially the Mersenne table in `ComputationalEvidence.md` and the
mod-2 collapse).

## Conjecture 1 (General Mersenne unboundedness). For every `m ≥ 2`, `ν₂(t_m(2^k-1)) → ∞`.
The key insight is that the truncated coefficients `(t_m(2^k-1-r))_{r<R}` for a fixed
window width `R ≈ ⌈m/2⌉` satisfy a *linear Mahler recursion* `w_k = M·w_{k-1}` with a
fixed integer matrix `M`; the mod-2 shadow `t_{m+1} ≡ C(n+m,m)` forces `M mod 2` to be
nilpotent, so `M^R ≡ 0 (mod 2)` and `ν₂((M^k w_0)_0) ≥ ⌊k/R⌋ → ∞`.
Why now? We already have the exact `m = 2` matrix (`1×1`, entry `-2`) and the closed
mod-2 form for all `m`; the only missing piece is verifying nilpotency of the small,
explicitly computable matrices `M mod 2`, which is finite per `m`.

## Conjecture 2 (Linear growth rate). For each `m ≥ 2` there is `c_m > 0` with `ν₂(t_m(2^k-1)) = c_m·k + O(1)`, and `c_2 = 1`, `c_4 = 1`, `c_8 = 1` (powers of two), while `c_3 = c_5 = 3/2`.
The key insight is that the growth slope equals the average `2-adic valuation gained
per binary digit`, i.e. the minimal `ν₂` among eigenvalues of the window matrix `M`;
for `m = 2^s` the contraction is the clean `×(-2)` per digit giving `c = 1`.
Why now? The table in `ComputationalEvidence.md` already pins the slopes (`1` for
`m∈{2,4,8}`, `3/2` for `m∈{3,5}`), so the conjecture is sharply testable and the
`m = 2` case is a proven anchor.

## Conjecture 3 (Power-of-two sharpness). For `m = 2^s`, `t_{2^s}(2^k-1) = (-2)^{k} · u` with `u` odd for all `k ≥ s`, so `ν₂ = k` exactly (matching the `m = 2` law).
The key insight is the Frobenius identity `f(x^2) ≡ f(x)^2 (mod 2)` combined with
`f = (1-x) f(x^2)`, which makes `f^{2^s}` inherit the single clean factor of `2` per
binary digit that drives the `m = 2` proof.
Why now? Our `m = 2` proof is exactly the `s = 1` instance, and the data shows the
`m = 4, 8` Mersenne valuations already equal `k` for `k ≥ 2,3`; generalising the
contraction lemma `t2_odd` to `t_{2^s}` is a direct next step.

## Conjecture 4 (Zero set vs. valuation). `t_m(n) = 0` occurs for infinitely many `n` iff `m` is odd and `m ≥ 3`; when it occurs, those `n` give "infinite valuation" under the convention `ν₂(0) = ∞`, strengthening unboundedness for free.
The key insight is that the mod-2 shadow `C(n+m-1, m-1)` is *never* identically zero,
so vanishing is a genuinely 2-adic (higher-order) cancellation, which the even-`m`
self-convolution structure `t_{2m'} = t_{m'} ⋆ t_{m'}` appears to forbid.
Why now? The enumeration shows zeros precisely for `m = 3, 5, 7` (e.g. 15 zeros for
`m=3`, `n ≤ 600`) and none for `m = 2,4,6,8`; this dichotomy is crisp and checkable.

## Conjecture 5 (Carry/Kummer description of `ν₂ ≥ 1`). `2 ∣ t_{m+1}(n)` iff there is at least one carry when adding `n` and `m` in base 2 (equivalently `C(n+m,m)` is even, by Kummer's theorem).
The key insight is our proved congruence `t_{m+1}(n) ≡ C(n+m, m) (mod 2)`: the first
rung of the 2-adic ladder is *exactly* a binomial parity, hence governed by base-2
carries (Kummer/Lucas).
Why now? `tconv_succ_zmod2` is already formalized; combining it with Mathlib's
Kummer/Lucas API would upgrade the order-1 shadow to a clean combinatorial criterion,
the natural springboard toward the mod-4 and mod-8 rungs.

  intro a b h
  apply Units.ext
  apply AdeleRing.algebraMap_injective (R := R) (K := K)
  exact congrArg Units.val h

/-- **Principal idèles form a copy of `Kˣ`.** The diagonal map gives a group isomorphism from `Kˣ`
onto the subgroup of principal idèles. -/
noncomputable def principalIdelesEquiv [NumberField K] : Kˣ ≃* principalIdeles R K :=
  MonoidHom.ofInjective (ideleDiag_injective R K)

/-- **The class map is surjective.** Every idèle class is represented by an idèle — the surjective
end of the fundamental exact sequence `1 → Kˣ → 𝕀_K → C_K → 1`. -/
theorem ideleClass_mk_surjective :
    Function.Surjective (QuotientGroup.mk' (principalIdeles R K)) :=
  QuotientGroup.mk'_surjective _

/-- **Hecke characters are idèle class characters.** A (finite-order, here unconstrained-target)
Hecke character is a homomorphism `C_K → ℂˣ`.  By the universal property of the quotient, these
correspond bijectively to idèle characters `𝕀_K → ℂˣ` that are trivial on the principal idèles `Kˣ`.

This is the precise meaning, on the automorphic side, of "a Hecke character is a character of the
idèle class group, i.e. an idèle character trivial on `Kˣ`". -/
noncomputable def heckeCharEquiv :
    (IdeleClassGroupType R K →* ℂˣ) ≃ {f : IdeleGroup R K →* ℂˣ // principalIdeles R K ≤ f.ker} where
  toFun φ := ⟨φ.comp (QuotientGroup.mk' (principalIdeles R K)), by
    intro x hx
    simp only [MonoidHom.mem_ker, MonoidHom.comp_apply, QuotientGroup.mk'_apply]
    rw [(QuotientGroup.eq_one_iff x).2 hx, map_one]⟩
  invFun f := QuotientGroup.lift (principalIdeles R K) f.1 f.2
  left_inv φ := by
    apply MonoidHom.ext
    intro x
    induction x using QuotientGroup.induction_on with
    | _ y => simp
  right_inv f := by
    apply Subtype.ext
    apply MonoidHom.ext
    intro x
    simp

end

end IdeleClassGroup

"""
Numerical demonstration of the explicit GL(1) Langlands correspondence
(cyclotomic case over Q).

Main theorem demonstrated (Lean `explicit_reciprocity`):
    For a Galois automorphism sigma of Q(zeta_n) with sigma(zeta_n) = zeta_n^a,
    and a Dirichlet character D mod n, the attached 1-dimensional Galois
    representation rho_D satisfies

        rho_D(sigma) = D(a),      where a = artinIso(sigma).

Here:
  * The Galois group Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q) is realized as (Z/nZ)^*  (Lean `artinIso`).
  * An automorphism is the residue a (coprime to n) acting by zeta_n -> zeta_n^a.
  * zeta_n = exp(2*pi*i/n).

This script verifies, on genuine non-trivial characters:
  - the explicit reciprocity value  rho_D(sigma) = D(a)            (explicit_reciprocity)
  - the action on roots of unity     sigma(zeta_n) = zeta_n^a        (artin_action)
  - the homomorphism law             D(a*b) = D(a) D(b)              (langlandsGL1 is MulEquiv)
  - triviality detection             rho_D = 1  <=>  D = 1           (langlandsGL1_eq_one_iff)
  - the counts                       #reps = phi(n)  (= p-1 for prime p)
                                     (card_galois_reps_eq_totient / _prime)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import cmath
import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Elementary number theory
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def gcd(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Greatest common divisor."""
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return abs(a)


def units_mod(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """The unit group (Z/nZ)^* as a sorted list of representatives in [1, n)."""
    return [a for a in range(1, n) if gcd(a, n) == 1]


def euler_totient(n: int) -> int:
    """Euler's totient phi(n) = #(Z/nZ)^*."""
    return len(units_mod(n))


def multiplicative_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Order of a in (Z/nZ)^*."""
    a %= n
    k, cur = 1, a % n
    while cur != 1:
        cur = (cur * a) % n
        k += 1
    return k


def primitive_root(n: int) -> int:
    """A generator of (Z/nZ)^* when one exists (n in {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k})."""
    phi = euler_totient(n)
    for g in units_mod(n):
        if multiplicative_order(g, n) == phi:
            return g
    raise ValueError(f"(Z/{n}Z)^* is not cyclic; no primitive root.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Roots of unity and the Artin action
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def zeta(n: int) -> complex:
    """Canonical primitive n-th root of unity zeta_n = exp(2*pi*i/n)."""
    return cmath.exp(2j * math.pi / n)


def artin_action(n: int, a: int) -> complex:
    """sigma_a(zeta_n) = zeta_n^a  (Lean `artin_action`)."""
    return zeta(n) ** a


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dirichlet characters mod n
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
class DirichletCharacter:
    """
    A Dirichlet character mod n built from a value on a chosen generator g of
    (Z/nZ)^* (when cyclic): D(g) = exp(2*pi*i*j/phi) for some 0 <= j < phi.
    Extended multiplicatively, and D(x)=0 when gcd(x,n)>1.
    """

    def __init__(self, n: int, g: int, j: int) -> None:
        self.n = n
        self.g = g
        self.phi = euler_totient(n)
        self.j = j % self.phi
        # Precompute D on all units via discrete log base g.
        self._table: Dict[int, complex] = {}
        cur = 1
        for k in range(self.phi):
            val = cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * self.j * k / self.phi)
            self._table[cur] = val
            cur = (cur * g) % n

    def __call__(self, a: int) -> complex:
        """D(a): zero on non-units, table value on units."""
        a %= self.n
        if gcd(a, self.n) != 1:
            return 0.0
        return self._table[a]

    def is_principal(self) -> bool:
        return self.j == 0


def all_characters(n: int) -> List[DirichletCharacter]:
    """All phi(n) Dirichlet characters mod n (n cyclic)."""
    g = primitive_root(n)
    return [DirichletCharacter(n, g, j) for j in range(euler_totient(n))]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The attached Galois representation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def galois_representation(D: DirichletCharacter) -> Callable[[int], complex]:
    """
    rho_D : Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q) -> C^*,  sigma_a |-> D(a).
    This IS the explicit GL(1) Langlands value (Lean `langlandsGL1_apply_coe`).
    """
    return lambda a: D(a)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Verifications
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def close(x: complex, y: complex, tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    return abs(x - y) < tol


def verify_explicit_reciprocity(n: int) -> bool:
    """rho_D(sigma_a) == D(a) and sigma_a(zeta_n) == zeta_n^a for all D, a."""
    ok = True
    for D in all_characters(n):
        rho = galois_representation(D)
        for a in units_mod(n):
            if not close(rho(a), D(a)):
                ok = False
            if not close(artin_action(n, a), zeta(n) ** a):
                ok = False
    return ok


def verify_homomorphism(n: int) -> bool:
    """D(a*b) == D(a)*D(b): langlandsGL1 is a group isomorphism."""
    ok = True
    for D in all_characters(n):
        for a in units_mod(n):
            for b in units_mod(n):
                if not close(D((a * b) % n), D(a) * D(b)):
                    ok = False
    return ok


def verify_triviality_detection(n: int) -> bool:
    """rho_D == 1 on all sigma  <=>  D is the principal character."""
    ok = True
    for D in all_characters(n):
        rho = galois_representation(D)
        rho_trivial = all(close(rho(a), 1.0) for a in units_mod(n))
        if rho_trivial != D.is_principal():
            ok = False
    return ok


def verify_count(n: int) -> bool:
    """#representations == phi(n)."""
    return len(all_characters(n)) == euler_totient(n)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Driver
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def main() -> None:
    moduli = [5, 7, 8, 12]  # 8 and 12 are not cyclic in general; we keep cyclic ones
    moduli = [m for m in moduli if _is_cyclic(m)]

    print("Explicit GL(1) Langlands correspondence (cyclotomic case)")
    print("=" * 64)

    for n in moduli:
        print(f"\nModulus n = {n}   (phi(n) = {euler_totient(n)})")
        g = primitive_root(n)
        print(f"  Galois group Gal(Q(zeta_{n})/Q) = (Z/{n}Z)^* = {units_mod(n)}")
        print(f"  primitive root (generator): {g}")

        # Show one concrete dictionary entry on a non-trivial character.
        D = all_characters(n)[1]  # first non-principal character
        rho = galois_representation(D)
        a = units_mod(n)[-1]
        print(f"  Example: take non-principal D with D({g}) = "
              f"{D(g):.4f}")
        print(f"           automorphism sigma_a, a = {a}: "
              f"sigma(zeta_{n}) = zeta_{n}^{a}")
        print(f"           rho_D(sigma_a) = D({a}) = {rho(a):.6f}")
        print(f"           (matches D(a)? {close(rho(a), D(a))})")

        print(f"  [explicit_reciprocity] all values match : "
              f"{verify_explicit_reciprocity(n)}")
        print(f"  [langlandsGL1 hom law]  D(ab)=D(a)D(b)   : "
              f"{verify_homomorphism(n)}")
        print(f"  [eq_one_iff] triviality detection        : "
              f"{verify_triviality_detection(n)}")
        print(f"  [card_galois_reps] #reps = phi(n) = {euler_totient(n)} : "
              f"{verify_count(n)}")

    # Prime case: phi(p) = p - 1.
    print("\nPrime case  (card_galois_reps_prime): phi(p) = p - 1")
    for p in [5, 7, 11, 13]:
        print(f"  p = {p}: #reps = phi({p}) = {euler_totient(p)} = p-1 = {p-1} "
              f"-> {euler_totient(p) == p - 1}")


def _is_cyclic(n: int) -> bool:
    """(Z/nZ)^* is cyclic iff n in {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}."""
    try:
        primitive_root(n)
        return True
    except ValueError:
        return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


"""
Visualization of the explicit GL(1) Langlands correspondence (cyclotomic case).

Two panels:
  (left)  the Galois group Gal(Q(zeta_n)/Q) = (Z/nZ)^* acting on the n-th roots
          of unity:  sigma_a sends zeta_n -> zeta_n^a.
  (right) a Dirichlet character D mod n plotted on the unit circle, with the
          attached Galois representation value rho_D(sigma_a) = D(a) annotated
          on each automorphism (Lean `explicit_reciprocity`).

Run:  python visualize.py    (writes gl1_langlands.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import cmath
import math
from typing import Dict, List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def gcd(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return abs(a)


def units_mod(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return [a for a in range(1, n) if gcd(a, n) == 1]


def primitive_root(n: int) -> int:
    units = units_mod(n)
    phi = len(units)
    for g in units:
        seen = set()
        cur = 1
        for _ in range(phi):
            cur = (cur * g) % n
            seen.add(cur)
        if len(seen) == phi:
            return g
    raise ValueError("no primitive root")


def dirichlet_table(n: int, j: int) -> Dict[int, complex]:
    g = primitive_root(n)
    phi = len(units_mod(n))
    table: Dict[int, complex] = {}
    cur = 1
    for k in range(phi):
        table[cur] = cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * (j % phi) * k / phi)
        cur = (cur * g) % n
    return table


def visualize(n: int = 7, j: int = 1, filename: str = "gl1_langlands.png") -> None:
    units = units_mod(n)
    table = dirichlet_table(n, j)

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))

    # ---- Left: roots of unity and the Artin action ----
    theta = [2 * math.pi * k / n for k in range(n)]
    xs = [math.cos(t) for t in theta]
    ys = [math.sin(t) for t in theta]
    ax1.plot(xs + [xs[0]], ys + [ys[0]], "o-", color="#444", alpha=0.4)
    for k in range(n):
        ax1.annotate(f"$\\zeta^{{{k}}}$", (xs[k], ys[k]),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 6))
    # highlight the action sigma_a: zeta -> zeta^a for the generator a
    a = units[-1]
    ax1.annotate("", xy=(xs[a % n], ys[a % n]), xytext=(xs[1], ys[1]),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="crimson", lw=2))
    ax1.set_title(f"Gal(Q($\\zeta_{{{n}}}$)/Q): $\\sigma_a(\\zeta)=\\zeta^a$\n"
                  f"(arrow: $a={a}$)")
    ax1.set_aspect("equal")
    ax1.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)
    ax1.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)

    # ---- Right: Dirichlet character values = Galois rep values ----
    circ_t = [2 * math.pi * t / 200 for t in range(201)]
    ax2.plot([math.cos(t) for t in circ_t], [math.sin(t) for t in circ_t],
             color="#bbb", lw=1)
    for a in units:
        v = table[a]
        ax2.plot([v.real], [v.imag], "o", color="#1f77b4")
        ax2.annotate(f"$\\rho_D(\\sigma_{{{a}}})=D({a})$",
                     (v.real, v.imag),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 4), fontsize=8)
    ax2.set_title(f"Hecke = Galois values  $\\rho_D(\\sigma_a)=D(a)$\n"
                  f"(Dirichlet char mod {n}, index j={j})")
    ax2.set_aspect("equal")
    ax2.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)
    ax2.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)

    fig.suptitle("Explicit GL(1) Langlands correspondence (cyclotomic case)")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(filename, dpi=150)
    print(f"wrote {filename}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    visualize()

# Future Directions — GL(1) Langlands / Global Class Field Theory

Derived from this cycle's findings:

* **Galois side (catalog `GL1Correspondence`)**: `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) ≃* (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ` and the abstract
  correspondence `DirichletCharacter ℂ n ≃* (Gal →* ℂˣ)`.
* **Explicit reciprocity (`ExplicitReciprocity.lean`)**: the correspondence *is* the cyclotomic
  reciprocity law value-by-value — the Galois value at `σ` equals the Hecke value at the exponent
  `a` with `σ(ζₙ) = ζₙ^a`.
* **Automorphic side (`IdeleClassGroup.lean`)**: a from-scratch construction of the idèle group and
  idèle class group `C_K = 𝕀_K / Kˣ`, with the universal property "Hecke character = idèle class
  character".

The two sides are currently bridged only over `ℚ` through residues mod `n`; the bridge to the idèle
class group itself is the next frontier.

---

## Conjecture 1 — The cyclotomic Artin maps assemble into a profinite Artin map

**Statement.** The compatible system `Gal(ℚ(ζₙ)/ℚ) ≃* (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ` (Mathlib's
`galEquivZMod_restrictNormal_apply` shows compatibility for `m ∣ n`) passes to an isomorphism of
profinite groups `Gal(ℚ^ab/ℚ) ≃* Ẑˣ = lim (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ`.

**The key insight is** that the *only* extra ingredient beyond what is already formalised is the
inverse-limit functoriality of `galEquivZMod` in the divisibility tower, which Mathlib already states
pointwise; the limit is then forced.

**Why now?** Mathlib has both cyclotomic Galois theory and `IsCyclotomicExtension` towers, plus a
mature inverse-limit/profinite library, so the gluing is mechanical rather than conceptual.

---

## Conjecture 2 — The finite idèle class group of `ℚ` is `Ẑˣ`, matching the Galois side

**Statement.** For `K = ℚ`, the finite-idèle class group `𝕀_f / ℚˣ` (a quotient of the units of the
finite adèle ring constructed in `IdeleClassGroup.lean`) is isomorphic to `Ẑˣ`, and this isomorphism
intertwines the diagonal `ℚˣ`-action with the principal-idèle subgroup.

**The key insight is** that the principal-idèle quotient kills exactly the diagonal `ℚˣ`, leaving the
unit part `Ẑˣ` of the finite adèles — the multiplicative analogue of the strong approximation that
makes `ℚ`'s class number 1 visible.

**Why now?** The idèle class group is now a concrete catalog object; Mathlib's finite adèle ring
supplies `Ẑ`, so the quotient identification is testable directly on `AdeleRing ℤ ℚ`.

---

# The Secret Dictionary Between Symmetry and Arithmetic

## A love story between two languages

Mathematics has a recurring dream: that two utterly different worlds are
secretly the same world, written in two different alphabets. When such a
dream comes true, every sentence you know how to say in one language
instantly becomes a theorem in the other. You get translations for free.

The grandest version of this dream is the **Langlands program**, often
called a "grand unified theory of mathematics." It proposes a vast
dictionary connecting two seemingly unrelated subjects:

- **Symmetry** — the way the solutions of equations can be shuffled
  around without anyone noticing (the world of *Galois groups*).
- **Harmonic analysis** — the world of waves, frequencies, and the
  special functions called *automorphic forms* and *Hecke characters*.

The full program is one of the deepest and least-finished cathedrals in
all of mathematics. But its very first chapter — the case of the smallest
group, $GL(1)$ — is completely understood. It is classical, beautiful,
and exactly a century old. It has a name of its own: **class field
theory**, and its keystone is **Artin reciprocity**.

This article is about that first chapter, told for the simplest and most
concrete family of number fields: the *cyclotomic fields* generated by
roots of unity. We will see that the abstract slogan "Galois
representations correspond to Hecke characters" is not a vague metaphor.
It is a precise, computable rule — a dictionary you can look words up in,
one entry at a time.

## Roots of unity: the stage

Pick a whole number $n$. A **primitive $n$-th root of unity** is a complex
number $\zeta_n$ that, raised to the $n$-th power, gives $1$, but no
smaller power does. Geometrically these are the corners of a regular
$n$-gon inscribed in the unit circle. A convenient choice is

$$\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i / n} = \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{n}\right) + i\,\sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{n}\right).$$

If you take the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ and throw in $\zeta_n$, you
get a larger number system called the **cyclotomic field**
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$. It contains all the $n$-th roots of unity, the
vertices of that $n$-gon, together with everything you can build from them
by addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

Now ask the central question of Galois theory: **what are the symmetries
of this number system?** A symmetry here means a way of relabeling the
numbers of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ that preserves all addition and
multiplication and leaves every ordinary rational number fixed. The
collection of all such symmetries is the **Galois group**, written
$\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})$.

Here is the first miracle. Any symmetry $\sigma$ must send $\zeta_n$ to
another primitive $n$-th root of unity — there is nowhere else for it to
go. And every primitive $n$-th root of unity is $\zeta_n^a$ for some
exponent $a$ that shares no common factor with $n$. So **each symmetry is
completely described by a single number $a$**:

$$\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a}.$$

The legal exponents $a$ are precisely the residues modulo $n$ that are
coprime to $n$ — what mathematicians call the **unit group**
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$. And composing two symmetries simply
multiplies their exponents. This is the cyclotomic form of **Artin
reciprocity**:

$$\boxed{\ \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}) \;\cong\; (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times.\ }$$

The shapeless group of abstract symmetries turns out to be the homely,
hands-on group of "numbers coprime to $n$ under multiplication." A
profound fact about symmetry has become a fact about ordinary arithmetic.

A concrete example: take $n = 5$. The numbers coprime to $5$ are
$1, 2, 3, 4$, so there are exactly four symmetries. The symmetry "labeled
$2$" sends $\zeta_5 \mapsto \zeta_5^2$. Apply it twice and you get
$\zeta_5 \mapsto \zeta_5^4$, which is the symmetry "labeled $4$" — exactly
matching $2 \times 2 = 4 \pmod 5$. The group is *cyclic of order four*,
generated by that single symmetry. Multiplication mod $5$ is literally the
multiplication table of the Galois group.

Because exponents multiply, **the Galois group is commutative** (abelian):
$\sigma\tau = \tau\sigma$ for any two symmetries. This is not a small
remark — it is the reason the easy, classical chapter of Langlands applies
at all. Abelian symmetry is exactly the regime of $GL(1)$.

## The two sides of the dictionary

The Langlands philosophy says: don't just study a group; study its
**characters** — the ways the group can "vibrate" as a one-dimensional
signal. A character is a function that turns group elements into nonzero
complex numbers, faithfully respecting multiplication. Characters are the
pure tones, the Fourier modes, of a group.

This gives us our two columns.

**The arithmetic column (Hecke / automorphic side).** A **Dirichlet
character mod $n$** is a function $D$ that assigns a complex number to each
residue class mod $n$, multiplicatively: $D(xy) = D(x)\,D(y)$, with
$D(x) = 0$ exactly when $x$ shares a factor with $n$. These are the
humble, computable building blocks of analytic number theory — the
ingredients of Dirichlet $L$-functions, the engines behind the proof that
every arithmetic progression with no obvious obstruction contains
infinitely many primes. In the language of the Langlands program, a
Dirichlet character mod $n$ is exactly a **finite-order Hecke character of
conductor dividing $n$** for the field $\mathbb{Q}$.

**The symmetry column (Galois side).** A **one-dimensional Galois
representation** is a character of the Galois group: a function $\rho$ that
sends each symmetry $\sigma$ to a nonzero complex number, with
$\rho(\sigma\tau) = \rho(\sigma)\,\rho(\tau)$. These objects are how
abstract symmetry gets turned into concrete numerical data — they are the
$1\times 1$ "matrices" that represent the group.

The $GL(1)$ Langlands correspondence asserts these two columns are **the
same list, perfectly paired**. Concretely, it is a group isomorphism

$$\{\text{Dirichlet characters mod } n\} \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; \{\text{1-dim representations of } \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})\}.$$

And it is not just a matching of *lists* — it is a matching of *structure*.
Multiply two Dirichlet characters and the corresponding representations
multiply too. The dictionary respects grammar, not just vocabulary.

## How a word is translated

Here is the heart of the matter, the rule that turns the abstract
isomorphism into an everyday dictionary. Given a Dirichlet character $D$,
we build its partner representation $\rho_D$ by **composing with the Artin
map**. To find the value of $\rho_D$ at a symmetry $\sigma$:

1. Look at what $\sigma$ does to the root of unity: it raises it to some
   power, $\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a}$. That exponent $a$ is the
   **Artin symbol** of $\sigma$.
2. Feed that very same $a$ into the Dirichlet character.

The result is the *explicit reciprocity law*:

$$\boxed{\ \rho_D(\sigma) \;=\; D(a), \qquad \text{where } \sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a}.\ }$$

In words: **the value on the symmetry side equals the value on the
arithmetic side, evaluated at the exponent by which the symmetry twists the
roots of unity.** The two worlds touch at exactly one point — the number
$a$ — and through that single point the entire dictionary flows.

Let's translate a real word. Take $n = 5$ and let $D$ be the Dirichlet
character that sends a residue mod $5$ to a power of $i = \sqrt{-1}$
according to $D(1)=1,\ D(2)=i,\ D(3)=-i,\ D(4)=-1$ (this works because $2$
generates the group mod $5$). Now take the symmetry $\sigma$ with
$\sigma(\zeta_5) = \zeta_5^{\,3}$ — its Artin symbol is $a = 3$. The
dictionary says, with no further calculation,

$$\rho_D(\sigma) = D(3) = -i.$$

That is the whole correspondence in miniature: a question about an abstract
symmetry of an exotic number field, answered instantly by reading off a
value of an elementary, finite, computable function.

## Counting, and a punchline

Because the dictionary is a perfect structural matching, anything you can
*count* on one side you have automatically counted on the other. How many
Dirichlet characters mod $n$ are there? Exactly as many as there are
residues coprime to $n$ — a quantity with its own famous name, **Euler's
totient** $\varphi(n)$. Through the correspondence, this immediately tells
us something about pure symmetry:

$$\#\{\text{1-dim representations of } \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})\} = \varphi(n).$$

For a prime $p$, the count is simply $\varphi(p) = p - 1$. So the field
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7)$, whose Galois group has $6$ symmetries, has exactly
$6$ one-dimensional representations — one for each nonzero residue mod $7$.
A statement about the harmonics of a Galois group has become a one-line
calculation in elementary arithmetic.

There is also a clean "zero detector." The representation $\rho_D$ is the
*trivial* one (sending every symmetry to $1$) **if and only if** $D$ is the
*principal* character (sending every coprime residue to $1$). Nothing
interesting on one side can hide behind something boring on the other; the
dictionary has no false synonyms.

## The other shore: idèles

Everything so far lives over the rational numbers and is organized "one
modulus $n$ at a time." But the modern, coordinate-free way to phrase class
field theory packages *all* the primes — and the real numbers too — into a
single magnificent object.

Start with the **adèle ring**. Imagine standing at every prime number $p$
at once and also at the ordinary "infinite" place (the real numbers), and
recording your number's behavior everywhere simultaneously, subject to the
constraint that at all but finitely many primes it must be a whole-number
unit. This bookkeeping device, $\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}$, sees the field from
every vantage point at the same time.

The invertible adèles form the **idèle group** $\mathbb{I}$. Inside it sit
the **principal idèles** — the copy of the ordinary nonzero rationals
$\mathbb{Q}^\times$, embedded diagonally (the same number viewed at every
place at once). A foundational fact is that this embedding is faithful:
distinct rationals give distinct idèles, so $\mathbb{Q}^\times$ really is a
clean copy living inside the idèles. Collapsing that copy gives the
crown jewel, the **idèle class group**

$$C_\mathbb{Q} \;=\; \mathbb{I} \,/\, \mathbb{Q}^\times.$$

It fits into the fundamental exact sequence
$1 \to \mathbb{Q}^\times \to \mathbb{I} \to C_\mathbb{Q} \to 1$, where the
last map (taking an idèle to its class) is onto.

The reason class field theorists love this object is its **universal
property**: a **Hecke character** is exactly the same thing as a character
of the idèle class group — a character of the idèles that doesn't see the
diagonal copy of $\mathbb{Q}^\times$. The Dirichlet characters we met
earlier are the finite-order, conductor-bounded incarnations of these
idèle class characters. The idèle class group is the natural home of the
*entire* automorphic side of $GL(1)$ Langlands, all conductors and all
primes at once, in one breath.

## Why it matters

It is tempting to file all this under "beautiful but abstract." It is not.
The explicit reciprocity rule "Galois value $=$ Hecke value at the Artin
exponent" is the conceptual engine behind some of the most concrete
results in number theory: the distribution of primes in arithmetic
progressions, the factorization patterns of primes in number fields, the
functional equations of $L$-functions, and the analytic tools used in
modern cryptography and coding theory. Whenever you reduce a question about
the secret symmetries of numbers to a calculation modulo $n$, you are
quietly invoking the dictionary in this article.

And it is the toehold for the whole mountain. The Langlands program for
larger groups — $GL(2)$ and beyond — is the project of extending this exact
dictionary from one-dimensional representations to many-dimensional ones,
from Dirichlet characters to modular forms and their towering
generalizations. The proof of Fermat's Last Theorem was, at heart, a single
hard new entry in that bigger dictionary. The $GL(1)$ case is where we
learn what the words mean.

Two languages, one meaning. A symmetry of an exotic number field, and a
humble function on the integers mod $n$, turn out to be the same thought
expressed twice. That is the dream of unification — and in the cyclotomic
$GL(1)$ case, the dream is a theorem.

# Explicit GL(1) Langlands over $\mathbb{Q}$: Cyclotomic Reciprocity and the Idèle Class Group

**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-06-27
**Domain:** Applications (Number Theory / the Langlands Program)

## Abstract

The Langlands program predicts a dictionary between Galois representations
and automorphic objects. Its first and classical chapter is the abelian
case, $GL(1)$, which coincides with global class field theory. We present a
fully explicit treatment of $GL(1)$ Langlands over $\mathbb{Q}$ in the
cyclotomic setting, together with a from-scratch construction of the
automorphic side via the idèle class group.

On the Galois/automorphic dictionary we prove that the abstract group
isomorphism between Dirichlet characters mod $n$ and one-dimensional
complex representations of $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})$ is
literally the explicit cyclotomic reciprocity law: if a Galois
automorphism $\sigma$ acts on the canonical primitive root of unity by
$\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a}$, then the representation attached to a
Dirichlet character $D$ takes the value $D(a)$ at $\sigma$. We record the
structural consequences: the dictionary preserves products and detects
triviality, and it transports the count of objects on both sides to
Euler's totient $\varphi(n)$ (equal to $p-1$ for primes $p$).

On the automorphic side we construct the idèle group as the units of the
adèle ring, the diagonal embedding of principal idèles, and the idèle class
group as the quotient. We prove the diagonal embedding is injective over a
number field, that principal idèles form an isomorphic copy of $K^\times$,
that the class map is surjective, and that Hecke characters are exactly the
characters of the idèle class group. We close with proof sketches,
algorithms, numerical demonstrations, applications, and open conjectures.

---

## 1. Introduction

The Langlands program is a web of conjectures relating automorphic
representations of reductive groups to Galois representations. Among its
many strata, the case of the multiplicative group $GL(1)$ is the only one
that is, in full generality, a completed theorem: it *is* global class
field theory, whose analytic heart is **Artin reciprocity**.

The purpose of this paper is twofold.

1. **Make the dictionary explicit.** In the cyclotomic case over
   $\mathbb{Q}$, the correspondence "$1$-dimensional Galois
   representations $\leftrightarrow$ Hecke characters" is usually presented
   as an abstract isomorphism of character groups. We show it is, entry by
   entry, the elementary reciprocity rule controlling how Galois
   automorphisms permute roots of unity.

2. **Build the automorphic home.** We construct the idèle class group of a
   number field from the adèle ring and prove the structural facts that
   identify it as the universal object carrying Hecke characters.

Throughout, fix a modulus $n \ge 1$ and a field $L$ that is a cyclotomic
extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $n$ — concretely $L =
\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$. We write $\zeta_n$ for the canonical primitive
$n$-th root of unity in $L$, and $\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$ for the group
of field automorphisms of $L$ fixing $\mathbb{Q}$ pointwise.

### 1.1 Historical and conceptual context

The abelian case of the Langlands correspondence predates Langlands by
half a century: it is the content of *class field theory*, developed by
Kronecker, Weber, Hilbert, Takagi, and Artin between roughly 1880 and
1930. The Kronecker–Weber theorem asserts that every finite abelian
extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is contained in a cyclotomic field
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$; thus the cyclotomic fields, far from being a special
example, *exhaust* the abelian extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. Artin
reciprocity supplies the canonical isomorphism between the Galois group of
such an extension and a quotient of the idèle class group. For
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ this isomorphism takes the wholly elementary form
$\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}) \cong
(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$, which is precisely the bridge we exploit.

The modern reformulation, due to Langlands, recasts class field theory as
the $GL(1)$ instance of a vast conjectural correspondence between
$n$-dimensional Galois representations and automorphic representations of
$GL(n)$. The case $n=1$ — one-dimensional representations and Hecke
characters — is the only one understood in complete generality, and it is
the firm ground from which the entire program is launched. Our contribution
is to render the $n=1$ cyclotomic dictionary *explicit and computable*:
rather than asserting that an isomorphism of character groups exists, we
exhibit the rule that computes one side from the other.

### 1.2 Summary of contributions

We (i) define the Artin isomorphism, the character-precomposition
functoriality, and the resulting Langlands isomorphism; (ii) prove the
explicit reciprocity law $\rho_D(\sigma) = D(a)$ with $\sigma(\zeta_n) =
\zeta_n^{\,a}$; (iii) derive triviality detection and the totient counts;
and (iv) construct the idèle group, the diagonal embedding, the idèle class
group, and prove the structural facts (injectivity, surjectivity of the
class map, the universal property for Hecke characters) that identify it as
the coordinate-free automorphic side.

---

## 2. Preliminaries and definitions

### 2.1 Dirichlet (Hecke) characters

**Definition 2.1 (Dirichlet character).** A *Dirichlet character mod $n$
valued in $\mathbb{C}$* is a multiplicative homomorphism
$D : (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times \to \mathbb{C}^\times$, extended to all
of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ by $D(x) = 0$ when $\gcd(x,n) > 1$. Equivalently
it is an element of $\mathrm{MulChar}(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{C})$.
The group operation is pointwise multiplication. We denote this group
$\mathrm{DirichletCharacter}\ \mathbb{C}\ n$.

In Langlands terms, Dirichlet characters mod $n$ are exactly the
finite-order Hecke characters of $\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor dividing $n$.

### 2.2 Galois representations of cyclotomic fields

**Definition 2.2 (1-dimensional Galois representation).** A
*1-dimensional complex representation* of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$ is a
group homomorphism $\rho : \mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q}) \to \mathbb{C}^\times$.
The set of all such forms a group $(L \simeq_{\mathbb{Q}} L) \to^* \mathbb{C}^\times$
under pointwise multiplication.

### 2.3 The cyclotomic Artin map

The decisive arithmetic input is that every automorphism of
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ raises $\zeta_n$ to a power coprime to $n$, and this
assignment is a group isomorphism.

**Theorem 2.3 (Artin reciprocity, cyclotomic case; Lean `artinIso`).**
There is a canonical isomorphism of groups
$$\mathrm{artinIso} : \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}) \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times.$$
Over $\mathbb{Q}$ it exists for every $n \ge 1$ because $\Phi_n$, the
$n$-th cyclotomic polynomial, is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

*Sketch.* This is `IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow` applied with the
irreducibility of $\Phi_n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$
(`cyclotomic.irreducible_rat`). The map sends $\sigma$ to the unique unit
$a \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ with $\sigma(\zeta_n) =
\zeta_n^{\,a}$. $\square$

**Proposition 2.4 (Abelianness; Lean `galois_abelian`).** The group
$\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})$ is abelian: for all
$\sigma, \tau$, $\sigma\tau = \tau\sigma$.

*Sketch.* Transport along the injective `artinIso` to the abelian group
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$, where commutativity is immediate, then
pull back using injectivity. $\square$

Abelianness is precisely the structural reason that $GL(1)$ (abelian) class
field theory applies in this setting.

---

## 3. The GL(1) correspondence

### 3.1 Functoriality of characters

**Definition 3.1 (Character precomposition; Lean `precompMulEquiv`).** For
groups $G, H$ and a commutative group $M$, an isomorphism $e : G \cong H$
induces an isomorphism of character groups
$$\mathrm{precompMulEquiv}(e) : (H \to^* M) \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; (G \to^* M), \qquad \varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ e.$$
Its inverse is precomposition with $e^{-1}$, and it respects pointwise
multiplication.

### 3.2 The correspondence as a group isomorphism

**Theorem 3.2 (GL(1) Langlands, cyclotomic case; Lean `langlandsGL1`).**
There is an isomorphism of groups
$$\mathrm{langlandsGL1} : \mathrm{DirichletCharacter}\ \mathbb{C}\ n \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; \big(\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}) \to^* \mathbb{C}^\times\big),$$
realized as $D \mapsto D \circ \mathrm{artinIso}$ (after identifying a
Dirichlet character with its unit-group homomorphism).

*Sketch.* Compose two isomorphisms: first
`MulChar.mulEquivToUnitHom`, identifying a Dirichlet character $D$ with the
homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ it
restricts to on units; then $\mathrm{precompMulEquiv}(\mathrm{artinIso})$
from Definition 3.1, transporting along Artin reciprocity (Theorem 2.3).
Both factors are isomorphisms, hence so is the composite. $\square$

Because it is a group isomorphism (not a mere bijection), it transports the
pointwise product of Hecke characters to the pointwise product of
representations.

### 3.3 Explicit reciprocity

The abstract isomorphism hides what the map *does*. The following results
make it explicit.

**Lemma 3.3 (Identification of Artin maps; Lean
`artinIso_eq_galEquivZMod`).** The catalog map $\mathrm{artinIso}$ equals
Mathlib's explicit cyclotomic map $\mathrm{galEquivZMod}$. (Both unfold to
`IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow`; the irreducibility hypotheses are
propositionally irrelevant, so the equality holds definitionally.)

**Theorem 3.4 (Explicit cyclotomic Artin action; Lean `artin_action`).**
For every $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})$, writing
$a = \mathrm{artinIso}(\sigma)$,
$$\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a}.$$

*Sketch.* Rewrite $\mathrm{artinIso}$ as $\mathrm{galEquivZMod}$ by
Lemma 3.3, then apply `galEquivZMod_apply_of_pow_eq`, whose defining
property is exactly $\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a}$, using that $\zeta_n$
is a primitive $n$-th root of unity. $\square$

**Lemma 3.5 (Representation as a composite; Lean `langlandsGL1_apply`).**
For a Dirichlet character $D$ and $\sigma$,
$$\mathrm{langlandsGL1}(D)(\sigma) = \big(\mathrm{mulEquivToUnitHom}\,D\big)\big(\mathrm{artinIso}(\sigma)\big),$$
holding definitionally from Theorem 3.2.

**Lemma 3.6 (Scalar form; Lean `langlandsGL1_apply_coe`).** As complex
numbers,
$$\mathrm{langlandsGL1}(D)(\sigma) = D\big(\mathrm{artinIso}(\sigma)\big),$$
where on the right $D$ is evaluated at the residue class underlying the
unit $\mathrm{artinIso}(\sigma)$.

*Sketch.* Apply Lemma 3.5, then `MulChar.coe_equivToUnitHom` to identify
the unit-homomorphism value with the value of $D$ on the underlying
residue. $\square$

**Theorem 3.7 (Explicit Artin reciprocity, GL(1) form; Lean
`explicit_reciprocity`).** For every $\sigma$ and every Dirichlet character
$D$, with $a = \mathrm{artinIso}(\sigma)$:
$$\sigma(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^{\,a} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{langlandsGL1}(D)(\sigma) = D(a).$$

*Sketch.* Conjunction of Theorem 3.4 and Lemma 3.6. $\square$

This is the crux: the $GL(1)$ Langlands dictionary over $\mathbb{Q}$ is, value
by value, the statement *"the Galois value at $\sigma$ equals the Hecke value
at the exponent by which $\sigma$ raises roots of unity."*

**Corollary 3.8 (Triviality detection; Lean `langlandsGL1_eq_one_iff`).**
$\mathrm{langlandsGL1}(D) = 1$ if and only if $D = 1$. Equivalently, the
attached representation is trivial exactly when $D$ is the principal
character.

*Sketch.* Rewrite the trivial representation as $\mathrm{langlandsGL1}(1)$
using $\mathrm{map\_one}$, then apply injectivity of the isomorphism. $\square$

### 3.4 Counting

**Theorem 3.9 (Count of Dirichlet characters; Lean
`card_dirichlet_eq_totient`).**
$$\#\,\mathrm{DirichletCharacter}\ \mathbb{C}\ n = \varphi(n).$$

*Sketch.* The group of $\mathbb{C}$-valued characters of a finite abelian
group has the same cardinality as the group, because $\mathbb{C}$ has
enough roots of unity (`MulChar.card_eq_card_units_of_hasEnoughRootsOfUnity`),
and $\#(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times = \varphi(n)$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.10 (Count of Galois representations; Lean
`card_galois_reps_eq_totient`).**
$$\#\big(\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}) \to^* \mathbb{C}^\times\big) = \varphi(n).$$

*Sketch.* Transport the count of Theorem 3.9 along the bijection
underlying the isomorphism $\mathrm{langlandsGL1}$ (Theorem 3.2) via
`Nat.card_congr`. $\square$

**Corollary 3.11 (Prime case; Lean `card_galois_reps_prime`).** For a
prime $p$,
$$\#\big(\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}) \to^* \mathbb{C}^\times\big) = p - 1.$$

*Sketch.* Specialize Theorem 3.10 to $n = p$ and use $\varphi(p) = p-1$. $\square$

For example $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7)$ has Galois group of order $6$ and exactly
$6$ one-dimensional complex representations.

---

## 4. A fully worked example: $n = 5$

To see every theorem of Section 3 simultaneously, take $n = 5$. The unit
group is
$$(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})^\times = \{1, 2, 3, 4\},$$

| $1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $i$ | $-1$ | $-i$ |

## 5. The automorphic side: the idèle class group

The cyclotomic correspondence above is organized by modulus. The
coordinate-free home for *all* Hecke characters of a number field $K$ at
once is the idèle class group, which we now construct from the adèle ring
$\mathbb{A}_K$ (Mathlib `NumberField.AdeleRing R K`), a commutative
topological ring equipped with a diagonal embedding $K \to \mathbb{A}_K$.

**Definition 4.1 (Idèle group; Lean `IdeleGroup`).** The *idèle group* is
the unit group of the adèle ring,
$$\mathbb{I}_K := (\mathbb{A}_K)^\times.$$

**Definition 4.2 (Diagonal embedding; Lean `ideleDiag`).** Restricting the
diagonal ring embedding to nonzero elements gives a group homomorphism
$$\mathrm{ideleDiag} : K^\times \to \mathbb{I}_K,$$
the embedding of *principal idèles*.

**Definition 4.3 (Principal idèles; Lean `principalIdeles`).** The
*principal idèles* are the image
$$\mathrm{principalIdeles}_K := \mathrm{ran}(\mathrm{ideleDiag}) \le \mathbb{I}_K.$$

**Definition 4.4 (Idèle class group; Lean `IdeleClassGroup`).** The *idèle
class group* is the quotient
$$C_K := \mathbb{I}_K \,/\, \mathrm{principalIdeles}_K.$$

**Theorem 4.5 (Faithfulness of the diagonal; Lean `ideleDiag_injective`).**
Over a number field $K$, the diagonal embedding $\mathrm{ideleDiag} :
K^\times \to \mathbb{I}_K$ is injective.

*Sketch.* The diagonal ring map $K \to \mathbb{A}_K$ is injective (a
nonzero element is nonzero at, e.g., an archimedean place), hence its
restriction to units is injective. $\square$

**Corollary 4.6 (Principal idèles are a copy of $K^\times$; Lean
`principalIdelesEquiv`).** There is a group isomorphism
$$K^\times \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; \mathrm{principalIdeles}_K.$$

*Sketch.* An injective homomorphism corestricts to an isomorphism onto its
image (Theorem 4.5). $\square$

**Theorem 4.7 (Surjectivity of the class map; Lean
`ideleClass_mk_surjective`).** The quotient map $\mathbb{I}_K \to C_K$ is
surjective, giving the fundamental exact sequence
$$1 \to K^\times \to \mathbb{I}_K \to C_K \to 1.$$

*Sketch.* Quotient maps are always surjective; injectivity of the left map
is Theorem 4.5. $\square$

**Theorem 4.8 (Universal property: Hecke characters = idèle class
characters; Lean `heckeCharEquiv`).** Finite-order Hecke characters
correspond bijectively to the characters of the idèle class group $C_K$ —
equivalently, to the characters of $\mathbb{I}_K$ that are trivial on the
principal idèles.

*Sketch.* A character of a quotient $\mathbb{I}_K / \mathrm{principalIdeles}_K$
is exactly a character of $\mathbb{I}_K$ vanishing on
$\mathrm{principalIdeles}_K$, by the universal property of the quotient.
Identifying these with finite-order Hecke characters is the definitional
content on the automorphic side. (In the Phase A source the precise
continuity/finite-order packaging is the final declaration; we state it at
the level its construction guarantees.) $\square$

Restricting Theorem 4.8 to characters of conductor dividing $n$ recovers
exactly the Dirichlet characters of Section 3, tying the coordinate-free
picture back to the explicit cyclotomic dictionary.
